claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is primarily governed by increased kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion rather than by configurational entropy alone.
Chemical short-range order at the nanoscale mediates the increased barriers to atomic diffusion.
Changing the number and types of constituent elements changes the configurational entropy of the nanoalloys.
Nanoscale interfaces within the alloy particles act as barriers to atomic diffusion.
Chemical short-range order within the alloy particles acts as a barrier to atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy promotes local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering increases kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
Increased kinetic barriers to diffusion retard phase separation.
Increased kinetic barriers to diffusion retard oxidation.
Kinetic stabilization is dominant over direct thermodynamic stabilization by mixing entropy during high-temperature exposure.
Higher-configurational-entropy nanoalloys will have slower atomic diffusion than lower-configurational-entropy nanoalloys under identical high-temperature conditions.
Higher-configurational-entropy nanoalloys will show less phase separation than lower-configurational-entropy nanoalloys under identical high-temperature conditions.
Higher-configurational-entropy nanoalloys will show reduced oxidation relative to lower-configurational-entropy nanoalloys under identical high-temperature conditions.
The prediction is limited to particles with tightly controlled size distributions and processing conditions.
The prediction applies at temperatures high enough to activate atomic mobility but below melting.
